title: A little holy below, much from above
hookLine: Luzzatto's last rung: after effort, holiness comes as a gift
carry: holiness: begun by effort, finished as a gift
last: THE MERCIFUL ONE WANTS THE HEART.

cards: A seed goes into the ground on a spring morning. The gardener did the digging, the watering and the weeding, and she'll keep doing them. But no gardener can pull a sprout out of the dirt by hand.

At some point the work stops being hers, and something else happens on its own time. Rabbi Moshe Chaim Luzzatto spent a whole book on hard, careful work: watchfulness, zeal, cleanliness, the rungs you've been climbing.
Then, on the last rung, he says something that sounds almost like a gardener.

teach.b: Luzzatto's book is called The Path of the Just.

Its ladder comes from an older saying in the Talmud, in the name of Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair: Torah leads to watchfulness, watchfulness to zeal, and on up, through purity, piety, humility and the fear of sin, until the saying reaches holiness.
First, the command. Holiness isn't a word Luzzatto made up.
Leviticus says, in the verse this path met in Kedoshim: "Ye shall be holy; for I the LORD your God am holy." It's spoken to a whole people, not to a few saints. Second, the twist.
Luzzatto writes that holiness has two parts. Its beginning is effort: a person works to set themselves apart for God, in thought and in deed.
Its end is a gift: God, he says, grants the holiness that effort alone could never finish. The climb is yours; the summit is given. Third, the source.

teach.h: A LITTLE BELOW, MUCH FROM ABOVE.
teach.b: He leans on a line from the Talmud, in tractate Yoma: a person who makes himself a little holy below is made much holy from above. A little, then much. The proportion is the point.

Fourth, what it looks like. For Luzzatto, the holy person doesn't leave ordinary life. He describes even eating and working, for such a person, as acts that serve God, the way an offering on the altar did.
Holiness here isn't a cloud above the kitchen; it's the kitchen, lifted. Every rung below asked for more effort. This one asks for effort, and then for open hands.

how: Students of Mussar often read The Path of the Just slowly, a chapter at a time, sometimes aloud with a study partner, working on each trait in turn; its closing chapters on holiness are read as the goal the whole ladder points toward.

o: holiness kept for a few saints, apart from life
holiness begun by effort and finished as a gift
holiness earned in full by your own hard work

games.q: holiness is given — tap the pairs.
p: the ladder's saying in the Talmud

s: Luzzatto teaches that holiness is finished by effort alone
he says holiness begins with effort but is finished as a gift from God.
the Talmud says a little holiness below draws much from above
tractate Yoma: a person who makes himself a little holy below is made much holy from above.
for Luzzatto, the holy person leaves ordinary life behind
he describes even eating and working, for such a person, as service of God.

games.q: you've climbed every rung Luzzatto describes, through humility and the fear of sin. what happens at the top, in his telling?
o: you finish the work by yourself.
holiness is given to you as a gift.
you start the ladder over from the bottom.
games.why: Luzzatto says holiness begins with effort and ends as a gift. the person climbs; God grants what effort alone can't finish.

practice: Let one high aim come to mind, something you'd like your life to hold: more patience, more honesty, a gentler home, a deeper prayer, and name the one small step that's truly yours to take.

Picture taking it, then, on an out-breath, open your hands on your knees; whatever comes of the step isn't yours to force. If you pray, hand the rest over in your own words; if you don't, simply rest with your hands open.

wordCard.voice: Holiness is given. In Hebrew, kedushah: holiness, the last rung of Luzzatto's ladder, begun by effort and finished as a gift. Today's word.
